# Peak District National Park

Scroll down


## A land of two halves

**Immerse yourself in exploring famous hills, dramatic rock edges beside wild moorlands and tranquil dales all in one day.**

At more than 550 squares miles and the UK’s original national park, the Peak District provides a taste of the outdoors to millions. Considered by many as the spiritual home of the free access to the countryside we all enjoy today, the Peak District continues to provide a warm welcome to those seeking some of their first inspirational connections with nature.

- [@PeakDistrict](https://twitter.com/@PeakDistrict)
- [peakdistrictnationalpark](https://facebook.com/peakdistrictnationalpark)

## Key activities

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Thumbnail-1-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Be a trail blazer , Activity

With over 35 miles of traffic-free level, easy access and all-user trails, let us take you into the heart of the national park.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Thumbnail-2-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### On your bike , Activity

With your own wheels or from several bike hire centres amongst stunning scenery, there’s no better way to explore.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/www.visitpeakdistrict-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### It’s a cave, man , Activity

Get a different perspective on the Peak District by heading below the famous summits to discover a whole new underground world.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/MG_1662-2-1920x1080.jpg)

## Special qualities

10 reasons to visit the Peak District

The ‘Mass Trespass’ took place within what is now the Peak District’s boundary, a group of working-class pioneers paving the way for the countryside access we all enjoy today.

Our boundary takes in the counties of Derbyshire, Cheshire, Staffordshire, South & West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester.

We have over 1,600 miles of rights of way to explore across the ‘White Peak’ and ‘Dark Peak’ areas of the national park.

Kids (and adults too!) love travelling through the myriad tunnels of the Monsal Trail, a reminder of former days of steam running through our valleys.

Our resident wildlife includes bold and bugling red deer in the autumn, white mountain hares in winter, and the rare and enigmatic ‘mountain blackbird’ (the ring ouzel) on our rocky edges.

History abounds within our built heritage from inspiration for Charlotte Bronte at our North Lees Hall, to the iconic towers of the Derwent Dam flown over by the 617 ‘Dambusters’ squadrons on their training missions.

The Pennine Way – which stretches along the UK’s spine to Scotland, starts in the Peak District in Edale, at the Nags Head pub.

Our network of level and surfaced former railway line trails extends to more than 30 miles, allowing everyone to get into the heart of the Peak District, including with our own range of mobility hire equipment.

If adrenaline is your go-to day out, then expect world-class rock climbing and bouldering, plus cycle routes that have helped get some of our top Olympians games-ready.

Get a taste of Peak District living with craft ales brewed right alongside our rivers, puddings that have been to outer space, or fire your creativity with the annual well dressing festivals.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Infinite-gallery-1-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Infinite-gallery-2-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Infinite-gallery-3-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Infinite-gallery-4-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Infinite-gallery-5-900x600.jpg)

Adventure starts here, whatever your age

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Infinite-gallery-6-900x600.jpg)

Follow in the footsteps of generations past

# A place for pioneers

**As the UK’s original national park, our past stretches back almost a century – far beyond our nearly 70 years since designation.**

Our uplands played host to the ‘mass trespass’ events of the 1930s, whose pioneering spirit would go on to set the foundations for our protected landscapes and the public access we all enjoy today. Through devastating wild fires, history-making changes to our transport network that saw bustling steam railways fall silent, to war time secrecy as home to the Dambusters training sorties, the Peak District has often been at the heart of change in our culture and communities. Fast forward generations and today we welcome visitors from all corners of the globe and all walks of life. Our all-access trails bring a nationally-renowned outdoors experience to thousands – wherever you set your limits – and our climbing and cycling offer is good enough for our finest medal-winning athletes. With over 38,000 residents, community spirit remains at our heart – whether you want a taste of the Peak District, are ready to immerse yourself in our annual festivals or want to explore your creativity there’s always something around the corner. If you’re ready to re-connect with nature, then the Peak District is ready with a warm welcome.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/MwS-Parsley-Hay_c_Tom-Marshall-6-1920x1080.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Roaches-PDNP-580x580.jpg)

### Getting there

Trains from nearby cities of Sheffield and Manchester run into the heart of the Hope Valley (for Castleton, caves and the Pennine Way) and to Buxton just outside the national park boundary, but close to many popular areas. Buses travel into and throughout the Peak District from other nearby towns and cities including Nottingham and Derby, Macclesfield and Chesterfield. The Hope Valley Explorer is a seasonal bus service run in partnership with the National Park Authority, and usually operates from Easter and throughout the summer holidays (sorry, no service currently due to Covid-19 restrictions).

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/North-Lees-campsite-580x580.jpg)

### Getting there alternatives

As well as the above rail and bus services, international airports at East Midlands and Manchester are less than an hour’s travel to the national park, with locations such as Birmingham, Liverpool, Leeds and Doncaster Robin Hood airports just a little further.

FEATURED

Peak District National Park (shaded green) within England | | Area | 555sqmi (1,440km2) | | Designated | 17April1951(1951-04-17) | | Visitors | Over 13million[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-1) | | Administrator | Peak District [National Park Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Authority "National Park Authority") | | Website | [www.peakdistrict.gov.uk](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/) | | | The **Peak District** is an [upland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland "Highland") area in central-northern England, at the southern end of the [Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennines "Pennines"). Mostly in [Derbyshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derbyshire "Derbyshire"), it extends into [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"), [Greater Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Manchester "Greater Manchester"), [Staffordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staffordshire "Staffordshire"), [West Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Yorkshire "West Yorkshire") and [South Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Yorkshire "South Yorkshire"). It is subdivided into the [Dark Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Peak "Dark Peak"), [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") dominated by [gritstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gritstone "Gritstone"), and the [White Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Peak "White Peak"), a [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") area with valleys and gorges. The Dark Peak forms an arc on the north, east and west of the district, and the White Peak covers central and southern areas. The highest point is [Kinder Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinder_Scout "Kinder Scout") (2,087ft (636m)). Most of the area is within the **Peak District National Park**, a protected landscape designated in 1951.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-2) A 2021 report states that "the Park's own population numbers around 40,000 and supports an estimated 18,000 jobs, predominantly through farming, manufacturing and, inevitably, tourism".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-3) The area has been inhabited since the [Mesolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesolithic "Mesolithic") era; it was largely used for agricultural purposes until mining arose in the Middle Ages. During the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), several [cotton mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_mill "Cotton mill") were constructed in the area's valleys by [Richard Arkwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Arkwright "Richard Arkwright"). As mining declined, quarrying grew. Tourism came with the railways, spurred by the landscape, [spa towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spa_town "Spa town") and [Castleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castleton,_Derbyshire "Castleton, Derbyshire")'s show caves. ## Toponymy The upland area of the Peak District, centred around Derbyshire, has historically been known as Peakland and The Peak. The [Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle") of 924 AD recorded the region's name as Peaclond (meaning hill country in [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English")), home of the [Pecsaetan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pecsaetan "Pecsaetan") tribe. From the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance"), prominent authors (such as [Thomas Hobbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes "Thomas Hobbes"), [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe"), [Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys "Samuel Pepys") and [Charles Cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Cotton "Charles Cotton")) referred to the area as just The Peak.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-5) ## Geography The Peak District forms the southern extremity of the Pennines.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-6) Much of it is upland above 1,000 feet (300m), its highest point being [Kinder Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinder_Scout "Kinder Scout") at 2,087ft (636m).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Nuttall-7) Despite its name, the landscape has fewer sharp peaks than rounded hills, [plateaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau "Plateau"), valleys, limestone [gorges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canyon "Canyon") and gritstone [escarpments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escarpment "Escarpment") (the "edges").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Landscape-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Gritstone_Edges-9) The mostly rural area is surrounded by conurbations and large urban areas, including [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), [Huddersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huddersfield "Huddersfield"), [Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheffield "Sheffield"), [Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby "Derby") and [Stoke-on-Trent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke-on-Trent "Stoke-on-Trent").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Peak_District_visitor_destination-10) The formal boundaries of the [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park "National park") cover most of the [Dark Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Peak "Dark Peak") and [White Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Peak "White Peak"), but the wider, informal region known as the Peak District is less well defined.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-11) The Dark Peak is largely uninhabited [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") and gritstone escarpments in the northern Peak District and its eastern and western margins. It encloses the central and southern White Peak, which is where most settlements, farmland and limestone gorges are found.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Character_areas-13) Three of [Natural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_England "Natural England")'s [National Character Areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Character_Area "National Character Area") (NCAs) cover parts of it. The Dark Peak NCA includes the northern and eastern parts of the Dark Peak and the White Peak NCA most of the White Peak. The western margins of the Dark Peak are in the South West Peak NCA, sometimes considered a third area, where farmland and pastured valleys are found with gritstone edges and moorland.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Character_areas-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-South_West_Peak-14) Outside the park, the wider Peak District extends from the gritstone moorlands of the [South Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Pennines "South Pennines") to the north, separated approximately by the [Tame Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tame,_Greater_Manchester "River Tame, Greater Manchester"), [Standedge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standedge "Standedge") and [Holme Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holme_Valley "Holme Valley").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-15) It continues south and roughly ends at the [Weaver Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weaver_Hills "Weaver Hills") near the [Churnet Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Churnet "River Churnet").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-17) It often includes the area approximately between [Disley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disley "Disley") and Sterndale Moor, encompassing [Buxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buxton "Buxton")[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-18) and the [Peak Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_Dale "Peak Dale") corridor.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-19) It may also include some of the outer fringes and foothills, such as the Churnet[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-20) and [lower Derwent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Derwent,_Derbyshire "River Derwent, Derbyshire") Valleys,[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Slow_Travel_The_Peak_District-21) and the area approximately between [The Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cloud_(hill) "The Cloud (hill)") and [Mow Cop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mow_Cop "Mow Cop").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-22) Conversely, while the rural west of the [City of Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Sheffield "City of Sheffield") falls in the park boundaries, the urban area of the city is usually excluded,[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-23) alongside the other surrounding large urban areas. The rest of the region is surrounded by lowlands,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-24) including the [Cheshire Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire_Plain "Cheshire Plain")[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-25) and [Greater Manchester Built-up Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Manchester_Built-up_Area "Greater Manchester Built-up Area")[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-26) to the west. The [Derbyshire and Yorkshire Coalfields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Yorkshire_Coalfield "South Yorkshire Coalfield") lie to the east[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-27) while the lowlands of the [Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands "Midlands") are to the south, near the north of the [Trent Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Trent "River Trent").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-28) The national park covers 555 square miles (1,440km2),[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-Area-29) including most of the region in Derbyshire and extends into Staffordshire, Cheshire, Greater Manchester and South and West Yorkshire. Its northern limit is on a track near Deer Hill in [Meltham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meltham "Meltham"); its southernmost point is on the [A52 road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A52_road "A52 road") near [Ashbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashbourne,_Derbyshire "Ashbourne, Derbyshire"). The boundaries were drawn to exclude built-up and industrial areas; in particular Buxton and the quarries at the end of the Peak Dale corridor are surrounded on three sides by the park. [Bakewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakewell "Bakewell") and many villages are in the national park, as is much of the rural west of Sheffield. In 2010 it became the fifth largest national park in England and Wales.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-30) In the UK, designation as a national park means that planning and other functions are provided by a national park authority, with additional restrictions that enhance protection from inappropriate development. Land within this national park as in others is in a mix of public and private ownership.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-31) The [National Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Trust_for_Places_of_Historic_Interest_or_Natural_Beauty "National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty"), a charity that conserves historic and natural landscapes, owns about 12 per cent of the land in the national park.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District#cite_note-32) Its three estates ( [High Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Peak_Estate "High Peak Estate"), [White Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Peak_Estate "White Peak Estate") and [Longshaw](

The majority of these car parks have a Pay & Display system, [cashless payment by app](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/parking#appPayment) is also available. **Please be aware that due to the rural location of most of our car parks, payment may be by coin as well as by card. A small number of locations may be coin or card only, for technical connectivity or security reasons.** See our [car park locations in the Peak District](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/parking/parking-locations) page for more information. We have 2 car parks with publicly accessible [EV charging points](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/ev-charging-points "Peak District EV Charging Points"). These are Millers Dale Station and Parsley Hay, they both offer two [7kw PodPoint chargers](https://pod-point.com/products/driver/app "External link to https://pod-point.com/products/driver/app") with 4 charging sockets in total. We provide car parks to help handle the numbers of visitors to the National Park and reduce congestion. Fees from our Pay & Display car parks are re-invested into the care and protection of landscapes local to that area and visitor facilities the car parks serve. Some of our car parks are small and fill up early in the day. Please be prepared before your visit to have some alternative options in mind and any relevant postcodes. Wherever you are in the National Park please do not park on grass verges, on either side of double-yellow lines, by farm gates or other undesignated areas as this can reduce access for farm vehicles, the emergency services and damage protected habitats. * * * ## Parking permits We sell digital parking permits (annual and weekly). An annual permit is **£82** and a weekly permit **£21.50**. Parking permit holders can't be guaranteed a parking space, as the spaces get filled on a 'first come, first served' basis. Our annual permits apply to all forms of vehicle (excluding commercial coaches). Where a larger vehicle can use the car park, but is unable to fit within one car parking bay, then they must pay for the number of bays the vehicle takes up and ensure the vehicle does not obstruct the area for other users. If you are purchasing for a larger vehicle then you may wish to purchase two permits, or ensure you have the ability to purchase additional parking spaces if you use more than one marked space in our car parks. Our digital permits can be used by a maximum of 2 vehicles registered at the same address, you will need to ensure that the correct vehicle is selected at time of parking. **Digital permits are sold through RingGo our cashless parking operator.** The permit can be used from date of purchase, or pre-purchased to start within 14 days. The start date will be selected at time of purchase, no purchase can be back-dated so will need to be purchased prior to arrival in car parks to ensure access to signal. The digital permits can be purchased via the RingGo app, the [RingGo website](https://myringgo.co.uk/ "External link to https://myringgo.co.uk/") or via their automated telephone line. | Permit | RingGo Zone | Pricing | | --- | --- | --- | | Annual | 51799 | £82
(£78 plus £4 RingGo convenience charge) | | Weekly | 51798 | £21.50
(£20.50 plus £1 RingGo convenience charge) | You will require a RingGo account to make your purchase, once set up, you will be able to create a new parking session for either **annual permit (enter location 51799)** or **weekly permit (enter location 51798)**. If you are purchasing for a larger vehicle then you will need to do this on the RingGo website (rather than the app) so you can select the extra option 'vehicle larger than one bay'. If you have any issues purchasing the digital permit please contact our Customer and Democratic Support Team on 01629 816200 or email: [customer.service@peakdistrict.gov.uk](mailto:customer.service@peakdistrict.gov.uk?subject=Parking%20Permit) * * * ## Cashless payment by app All Peak District National Park Authority car parks requiring Pay & Display now offer a quick and easy alternative to pay by phone with [RingGo](https://myringgo.co.uk/ "External link to https://myringgo.co.uk/"), the UK’s no.1 parking app. ### Late Pay Locations There are a [small number of our car parks](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/parking/parking-locations) where we know signal is an issue and we therefore allow payment to be made within 24 hours of parking. When using these sites, please take a note of the location number and pay within 24 hours of your arrival to avoid any further action in relation to non-payment. Please also ensure that the parking period you purchase covers the time that your car was in the car park. For all other locations, a valid ticket, permit or blue badge must be on display or payment by phone submitted. ### How to use RingGo 1. Download the RingGo app - go to the App Store or Google Play Store and search for RingGo. 2. Set up an account by registering a few details so the next time you want to park, you can pay in seconds. 3. When you park in an area where RingGo is offered, you need to: - Confirm your vehicle registration number (with no spaces). - Enter the five or six-digit location number shown on signs at the location. For example, if there is a sign with ‘234567’ displayed, this is the location code you must use. - Select how long you want to stay. - Confirm your payment details. If your parking is running out, you can extend the time wherever you are by using the RingGo app. Select your current parking session from the sessions tab and the app will ask how long you want to extend. Choose a time, confirm and your parking is sorted. * * * ## Parking charges Charges apply between 9am and 6pm every day. Cash and Card payments are not available in all locations, so please be prepared for our coin only and card only machines. | Parking Tariffs | Charge (£) | | --- | --- | | Up to 1 hr | 2.10 | | Up to 2 Hr | 3.40 | | Up to 4 hr | 5.50 | | All day | 6.60 | | Coaches (where permitted) 3 hr | 6.10 | | Ilam Coach Bay: coaches and minibuses only | 20.00 | | Horse boxes/lorries up to 2 hr | 5.90 | | Horse boxes/lorries all day | 9.60 | | Motorcycles all day | 2.60 | | Blue Badge holders | Free | | Cycles | Free | | Weekly permit | 20.50 | | Annual permit | 78.00 | | [Parking charges for other providers' car parks](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/parking#other) | | * * * ## Parking restrictions ### Height and size restrictions None of our car parks have height restriction barriers in place, however some are not suitable for larger vehicles. Where a larger vehicle can use the car park, but is unable to fit within one car parking bay then they must pay for the number of bays the vehicle takes up and ensure the vehicle does not obstruct the area for other users, or may be subject to enforcement. ### Overnight parking Overnight parking or camping at all of our car parks is prohibited and may be subject to patrols and enforcement action. ### Disabled parking We aim to provide clear demarked/delineated disabled bays where car park surfaces allow. Car parks with dedicated spaces are listed below. Vehicles displaying a valid blue badge can park for free. ### Horse boxes Several car parks open onto trails or bridleways and are ideal for exploring the national park on horseback. Please ensure that you pay for the number of spaces you use and ensure that your vehicle is not obstructing the area for other users. * * * ## How do we use car park fees? - To maintain the car parks, trails, Stanage-North Lees and public toilets - Pay for litter removal (around 70 tonnes across the National Park each year) ### Related documents - [Bylaws for Car Parks](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/104814/PDNPA-Byelaws-Car-Parks-2024.pdf) (392KB) - updated November 2024 * * * ## Finding our car parks Our car parks have signage and tariff boards under Peak District National Park Authority, and have the millstone logo on them. Peak District National Park Authority parking permits are applicable in these car parks only, if you have a digital permit you must ensure that you have selected the correct registration for the parking session, or if you have a physical permit this must be clearly displayed within the vehicle when in use. Our annual and weekly permits  are the only publicly available permits that are eligible in our car parks, permits purchased from other providers are not eligible. We are unable to accept responsibility for fees or penalty charges incurred in facilities we do not manage. * * * ## ANPR Trial at Millers Dale We are trialling ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition) cameras at our car park at Millers Dale from 1 December 2026.  These cameras will be linked to our existing payment methods, the pay and display machines and RingGo, so if you pay for the parking session recorded by either of these means you do not need to do anything else. All permit holders have been contacted to ask for registrations to be used at Millers Dale, if you haven’t returned yours, please email [carparks@peakdistrict.gov.uk](mailto:carparks@peakdistrict.gov.uk) with your permit number and up to 3 registrations you may use there. If you are a Blue Badge holder, you can still park for free at Millers Dale provided you have your Blue Badge displayed, and visit the link (address) to record your registration number and Blue Badge number within 24 hours of parking. In line with good practice there will be at least a 10-minute observation period for you to decide whether you wish to park in the car park or leave.  The timestamped cameras will not issue Notices for any stay under 10 minutes. Please remember that there is no overnight parking within any of our car parks, and we will be using the ANPR cameras to enforce this at Millers Dale.  The car parks are closed between midnight and 6am, as detailed within the car park Byelaws and terms and conditions. * * * ## Other provider car parks For other car parks in the Peak District please visit the relevant website: - [National Trust](https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/days-out/regionmidlands/the-peak-district) - [Severn Trent Water](https://www.stwater.co.uk/wonderful-on-tap/our-visitor-sites/come-visit-us/) - [Forestry Commission](https://www.forestry.gov.uk/) - [Derbyshire County Council](http://www.derbyshire.gov.uk/transport_roads/roads_traffic/parking/default.asp) - [Derbyshire Dales District Council](https://www.derbyshiredales.gov.uk/community-a-living/parking/car-park-locations) - [High Peak Borough Council](https://www.highpeak.gov.uk/article/706/Parking) #### Share this page - [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/parking "Share on Facebook") - [Share on X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Park%20and%20protect%20-%20our%20car%20parks%20-%20https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/parking "Share on X") - [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/visiting/planning-your-visit/parking&title=Park%20and%20protect%20-%20our%20car%20parks "Share on LinkedIn") - [Email to a friend](https://www.peakdistrict.gov.uk/home/send-to-a-friend-page/send-to-a-friend?asset_to_send=65988)
